rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window for all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
All pairs have excess resolution, so double the gradient slope to reduce the time penalty. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed will show how the critical pairs respond to slope.
Test whether higher temperature separates the compressed middle cluster while preserving the short run. Holding the gradient fixed isolates temperature-dependent selectivity changes.

Test an intermediate temperature to avoid the near-coelution at 60 C while shifting the critical middle cluster away from its 40 C overlap. The last peak should remain within the zero-time-penalty region.

The middle pair separates as temperature rises, but another pair converges near 60 C. Test 55 C with a slightly steeper gradient to shift these competing selectivity constraints while keeping the time penalty at zero.

At 55 C, lengthen the gradient from 8 to 10 minutes to improve the newly critical pair. This also directly tests the temperature midway between injections 4 and 3 while retaining a short elution time.

The critical pair improved substantially when tG increased from 8 to 10 minutes; another two minutes may bring it above R = 1.5. The projected last-peak time is about 7.6 minutes, potentially preserving the zero time penalty.

Injection 7 already achieved the maximum CRF and remains the best method. Test a slightly higher starting organic fraction to see whether a shifted gradient window improves the narrow resolution margins while retaining zero time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 8 to improve its critical pair while keeping the last peak near 7.6 minutes. This may recover CRF 1.000 with more balanced resolution margins; injection 7 remains the established optimum.

Reduce the endpoint another grid step to bring the R = 1.47 pair above 1.5 while potentially keeping the last peak near the zero-penalty boundary. Injection 7 already attains the maximum score and remains the fallback.

Test a slightly shallower gradient adjacent to injection 7 to map the maximum-score region. It should improve the R = 1.59 pair, though the R = 1.52 pair and last-peak time may approach their scoring boundaries.
The maximum CRF is already secured at 55 C. Test the unexplored low-temperature limit with the short gradient to look for an alternative selectivity window with larger resolution margins.

With the maximum score already secured, test a faster, high-temperature selectivity window. A substantially steeper gradient may move the pair that nearly coeluted at 60 C past its crossover, although other pairs may become critical.

Return to the successful 55 C region and shift both gradient endpoints downward in slope while raising the starting fraction relative to injection 10. This tests whether the competing critical pairs can gain more balanced resolution margins near the zero-time-penalty boundary; injection 7 remains the established maximum-score method.

Lengthen injection 8's gradient to improve its slope-sensitive critical pair while retaining the favorable separation of the other middle pair. This tests a potentially better-balanced resolution margin near the time-penalty boundary; injection 7 already secures the maximum CRF.

Test the temperature sensitivity of injection 10, which achieved maximum CRF with slightly larger resolution margins than injection 7. Holding the gradient fixed will show whether that alternative tolerates a 5 C decrease; the established maximum-score methods remain available.

Preserve injection 7's gradient slope and temperature while ending the ramp earlier at a lower organic fraction. All peaks previously eluted before 10 minutes, so this distinct method should reproduce the maximum-score separation without requiring a 95% organic endpoint.

Test a slope between injections 9 and 10 to balance their competing critical pairs, targeting minimum resolution near 1.6 with the last peak around 7.8 minutes. This may retain maximum CRF with better resolution margins than injection 7.

Test a shorter ramp followed by a hold: the middle peaks should retain injection 7's gradient slope but experience the higher starting fraction. The 55% organic hold should still elute the last compound promptly, testing whether a lower endpoint can support a maximum-score method.

Match injection 10's successful slope and starting composition with a shorter ramp ending at 60% organic. The last peak should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving the maximum-score separation with a lower endpoint.

Preserve injection 7's successful slope and temperature while trimming the endpoint to 65% organic. The last peak should still elute within the gradient, retaining maximum CRF with a shorter programmed ramp.

Keep the maximum-score gradient slope through the critical middle peaks, then hold at 50% organic. This tests whether the last compound can elute during the hold without incurring a time penalty; injection 21 remains the proven shorter-ramp optimum.

Test the upper-temperature sensitivity of injection 20's maximum-score method, complementing the 50 C test of its equivalent gradient slope. This will establish whether the improved resolution margins at 55 C survive a 5 C increase; the proven optimum remains unchanged.

Return to 55 C and slightly flatten injection 14's gradient to improve its R = 1.22 pair while retaining the other critical pair's larger margin. This tests the edge of the maximum-score region at a higher starting organic fraction; injection 7 remains the established optimum.

Use the final injection near the proven maximum-score region, with a slope just shallower than injection 15 to strengthen the slope-sensitive pair while likely keeping the other critical pair above 1.5. The last peak should remain near 8.3 minutes with no time penalty; injection 7 already secures the maximum achievable CRF.
